title.zh: 面部按摩美容：中医手法让容颜焕发
title.en: Facial Massage Beauty: TCM Techniques for Radiant Skin

description.zh: 掌握中医面部按摩的方法，促进面部气血流通，让容颜焕发光彩
description.en: Master TCM facial massage techniques, promote facial Qi-Blood circulation

zh.text: 面部按摩是中医美容的重要组成部分，其理论根源可追溯至《黄帝内经》中"经脉者，所以行血气而营阴阳"的核心思想。人体面部是诸阳之会，手足三阳经皆上行于面，面部气血的盛衰直接决定了皮肤的状态——红润或暗沉、紧致或松弛、光泽或枯槁。通过按摩面部特定穴位和循行经络，可以疏通气血、调和阴阳，让容颜由内而外焕发光彩。我在临床中观察到，坚持面部按摩的患者，其皮肤状态明显比同龄人更加年轻，这正是"经络通畅、气血得荣"的外在体现。
面部按摩的好处

面部按摩的好处远不止"舒服"二字。《灵枢·本藏》云："经脉者，所以行血气而营阴阳，濡筋骨，利关节者也。"面部按摩通过对穴位和经络的刺激，能够显著改善面部的气血运行。气血充足通畅，面色自然红润光泽。从现代医学角度看，按摩可以促进面部微循环、增加皮肤组织的营养供应、加速代谢产物排出，这与中国古代"流水不腐、户枢不蠹"的道理如出一辙。具体而言，面部按摩能改善血液循环从而淡化皱纹、延缓衰老；能促进面部气色、使面色红润有光泽；能通过促进水液代谢来消除面部浮肿；还能舒缓面部紧张的神经和肌肉，让人从内到外感到放松。
面部重要穴位
《针灸大成》曰："头面之穴，犹百川之汇海。"面部穴位虽然小巧，却是调畅面部气血的关键枢纽。我根据多年临床经验，将面部常用穴位按功效分为三类。
美白养颜穴位

四白穴位于眼眶下缘正中直下一横指处，《针灸甲乙经》记载其主治"目眩、目痛"，是面部美白的第一要穴。此穴属足阳明胃经，胃经多气多血，按揉四白穴能调动面部气血，使皮肤得到充分濡养。迎香穴在鼻翼外缘中点旁，鼻唇沟中，为手阳明大肠经和足阳明胃经的交会穴，按之可改善面色、通利鼻窍。颧髎穴在颧骨下缘凹陷处，是手太阳小肠经的穴位，长于淡化色斑。地仓穴在嘴角外侧约四分处，按揉可改善唇色、延缓口周衰老。这四穴常被古代宫廷美容方所用，至今依然实用。
抗衰老穴位
太阳穴是经外奇穴，位于眉梢与目外眦之间向后一横指的凹陷处，按揉可缓解眼疲劳、减少鱼尾纹。攒竹穴在眉头凹陷处，属于足太阳膀胱经，长于改善眼周气血循环、延缓眼周衰老。鱼腰穴在瞳孔直上、眉毛正中凹陷处，属于经外奇穴，按摩可改善眉间和额部皱纹。丝竹空穴在眉梢外侧凹陷处，属于手少阳三焦经，配合攒竹穴按摩可缓解眼周疲劳和细纹。我在临床中观察到，坚持按揉这四穴的中年以上患者，眼周皱纹的进展速度明显慢于同龄人。
舒缓放松穴位

印堂穴位于两眉之间正中，属于经外奇穴，《素问·刺热》以面色部位对应五脏，印堂区域可反映心肺功能，按揉此穴有安神定志之功。百会穴位于头顶正中线与两耳尖连线的交点，是诸阳之会，按揉可提升阳气、改善精神不振。风池穴位于后颈部、胸锁乳突肌与斜方肌上端之间的凹陷处，属于足少阳胆经，按揉可舒缓头颈疲劳。合谷穴虽然位于手背，但"面口合谷收"是针灸学的基本原则之一，按揉此穴可对面部问题起到整体调节作用，尤其适合自我保健。
面部按摩手法
中医按摩手法种类繁多，应用于面部时需以轻柔温和为原则。面部的皮肤和肌肉结构精巧、血供丰富，手法过重反而会损伤皮肤和毛细血管。我在临床中总结了一套适合居家操作的按摩手法。
基础按摩手法

推法：用食指和中指的指腹沿经络走向由下向上、由内向外推动，力度以不牵拉皮肤为度。揉法：用指腹在穴位上做轻柔缓和的环形揉动，速度不宜过快。按法：用指腹垂直按压穴位，力量由轻渐重，以局部出现酸胀感为度，持续5至10秒后缓慢放松。抹法：用食指和中指的指腹沿面部轮廓进行直线或弧线抹擦，常用于提拉面部线条。拍法：用双手手掌或指尖交替轻拍面部，频率稍快，力度轻柔，可持续拍打30至60秒，能有效促进面部血液循环。
面部按摩步骤

我推荐一套七步面部按摩法：第一步，彻底清洁面部后涂抹足量的按摩油或面霜，以减少摩擦。第二步，双手食指和中指并拢，从下巴正中沿下颌线向上推至耳前，重复10次，有提拉下颌轮廓的作用。第三步，从鼻翼两侧经过颧骨向太阳穴方向推抹，重复10次。第四步，用食指指腹按揉四白穴和迎香穴，各按揉18次。第五步，按揉太阳穴和攒竹穴，各按揉18次。第六步，用指腹轻拍全脸，从前额到下颌，持续30秒。第七步，用温热的毛巾敷面1至2分钟，促进血液循环和护肤品吸收。整套流程约10至15分钟，每日一次即可。
不同问题的按摩方法
面部按摩的精妙之处在于，针对不同的问题可以采取不同的按摩策略，做到"因人制宜、因症施术"。
淡化皱纹按摩
皱纹的出现在中医看来本质上是气血亏耗、皮肤失养的信号。眼周皱纹重在按揉攒竹穴和丝竹空穴，配合食指从内眼角向外眼角轻轻推抹。额头皱纹可从眉心（印堂穴）处用指腹向上交替推至发际线。嘴角下垂和口周纹路可重点按揉地仓穴，配合从鼻唇沟向两侧嘴角的推抹。法令纹是很多中年人的困扰，可从鼻翼根部沿鼻唇沟向下推至嘴角，反复多次。上述手法每周坚持5次以上，一般一个月左右即可看到纹理的改善。
美白淡斑按摩
色斑的形成多与肝郁、血瘀有关，按摩的目的在于疏通面部气血瘀滞。四白穴是美白第一要穴，每次按揉以酸胀为度。颧髎穴针对色斑区域重点按揉。迎香穴按揉可改善整体气色。此外，从面部正中向两侧沿经络方向推抹，有助于疏通瘀滞、促进代谢。需注意，按摩淡斑起效较慢，通常需要3个月以上的持续坚持，但一旦起效则效果稳定持久，这是外用美白产品难以比拟的。
消除浮肿按摩
晨起面部浮肿多因水液代谢不畅所致。消除浮肿的按摩要点是"由内向外、由下向上"的推抹手法——从面部中线向两侧推，从下颌向上推至太阳穴，配合轻拍面部，可有效促进淋巴回流和水液代谢。眼袋浮肿可按揉眼周穴位配合从内眼角向外眼角的轻抹。通常坚持按揉5至10分钟，浮肿即可明显消退。
面部按摩注意事项
面部按摩看似简单，但若操作不当反而有害。力度要适中——过重可能拉伤皮肤或导致毛细血管破裂，过轻则达不到刺激经络的效果。方向要正确——面部的按摩方向应顺应经络走向和淋巴回流方向，一般遵循"由下向上、由内向外"的原则，不可逆向操作。每次按摩时间以10至15分钟为宜，过长反而增加皮肤负担。每日1至2次即可，过度频繁并无益处。按摩前务必彻底清洁面部并涂抹润滑介质（按摩油或面霜），避免干推造成皮肤损伤。
最佳按摩时间
面部按摩的最佳时间有两个：一是早晨起床后。此时人体阳气初升，面部经过一夜休息后气血趋于平静，适度的按摩可以唤醒面部气血，让人精神焕发。二是睡前1小时。晚间按摩配合护肤产品，既能放松面部神经、有助于睡眠，又能促进护肤品成分的吸收。此外，长时间用电脑或工作疲劳后，用短短5分钟按揉太阳穴和印堂穴，能迅速缓解面部紧张。要提醒的是，饭后半小时内和皮肤有急性炎症或伤口时不宜进行面部按摩。
温馨提示：面部按摩需要长期坚持方能见效，三天打鱼两天晒网难以收到理想效果。皮肤有严重痤疮、皮炎、过敏或破损时不宜按摩。建议将面部按摩与内调体质相结合，内外兼修才能取得最佳的美容效果。

en.text: Facial massage is an essential component of TCM beauty practice, rooted in the core principle from the Huang Di Nei Jing that "meridians transport qi and blood to nourish yin and yang." The face is the meeting point of all yang meridians — the three hand-yang and three foot-yang meridians all ascend to the face. The abundance or deficiency of facial qi and blood directly determines skin condition: rosy or dull, firm or lax, radiant or withered. By massaging specific facial acupoints and following the meridian pathways, we can unblock qi and blood, harmonize yin and yang, and allow the complexion to radiate from within. In my clinical observation, patients who consistently practice facial massage show significantly younger skin compared to their peers — a visible manifestation of the principle that "when meridians are unblocked, qi and blood flourish."
Benefits of Facial Massage

The benefits of facial massage extend far beyond the feeling of relaxation. The Lingshu states: "Meridians transport qi and blood to nourish yin and yang, moisten tendons and bones, and facilitate joint movement." By stimulating acupoints and meridians, facial massage markedly improves qi and blood circulation to the face. When qi and blood are abundant and flowing smoothly, the complexion naturally becomes rosy and radiant. From a modern medical perspective, massage enhances facial microcirculation, increases nutrient supply to skin tissues, and accelerates metabolic waste removal — a principle that aligns perfectly with the ancient Chinese wisdom that "flowing water never stagnates, and a moving door hinge never rusts." Specifically, facial massage improves blood circulation to fade wrinkles and delay aging, enhances complexion for a naturally rosy glow, promotes fluid metabolism to eliminate facial puffiness, and relaxes tense facial nerves and muscles for a profound sense of relaxation.
Important Facial Acupoints

As the Great Compendium of Acupuncture states: "The acupoints of the head and face are like a hundred rivers converging into the sea." Although small in size, facial acupoints are crucial hubs for regulating qi and blood flow to the face. Based on years of clinical experience, I categorize the commonly used facial acupoints into three groups by function.
Whitening & Beauty Acupoints

Sibai (ST2), located directly below the pupil in the depression of the infraorbital foramen, is recorded in the Jia Yi Jing as treating "dizziness and eye pain" and is the foremost acupoint for facial whitening. It belongs to the Foot Yangming Stomach Meridian, which is abundant in qi and blood — massaging Sibai mobilizes facial qi and blood to fully nourish the skin. Yingxiang (LI20), beside the midpoint of the nasal ala in the nasolabial groove, is the meeting point of the Large Intestine and Stomach meridians — pressing it improves complexion and opens the nasal passages. Quanliao (SI18), in the depression below the cheekbone, belongs to the Small Intestine meridian and excels at fading pigmentation spots. Dicang (ST4), about 0.4 cun lateral to the mouth corner, improves lip color and delays perioral aging when massaged. These four points were frequently used in ancient palace beauty formulas and remain highly effective today.
Anti-Aging Acupoints

Taiyang (EX-HN5), an extra point located in the depression one finger-width behind the midpoint between the outer canthus and the eyebrow tail, relieves eye fatigue and reduces crow's feet when massaged. Cuanzhu (BL2), in the depression at the medial end of the eyebrow, belongs to the Bladder meridian and excels at improving periocular circulation and delaying eye area aging. Yuyao (EX-HN4), in the depression at the midpoint of the eyebrow directly above the pupil, is an extra point that improves forehead and glabellar wrinkles. Sizhukong (SJ23), in the depression at the lateral end of the eyebrow, belongs to the Sanjiao meridian — combined with Cuanzhu massage, it relieves periocular fatigue and fine lines. In my clinical observation, middle-aged and older patients who consistently massage these four points show significantly slower progression of periorbital wrinkles compared to their peers.
Relaxing Acupoints

Yintang (EX-HN3), located at the midpoint between the eyebrows, is an extra point. The Su Wen associates the Yintang area with heart-lung function — massaging it calms the spirit and settles the mind. Baihui (GV20), at the intersection of the midline of the head and the line connecting the apex of both ears, is the meeting point of all yang meridians — massaging it raises yang qi and improves lethargy. Fengchi (GB20), in the depression between the upper ends of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles at the back of the neck, belongs to the Gallbladder meridian and relieves head and neck tension. Hegu (LI4), though located on the dorsum of the hand, follows the classic acupuncture principle that "facial and oral disorders are treated with Hegu" — massaging it provides overall regulation of facial conditions and is especially suitable for self-care.
Facial Massage Techniques

TCM massage encompasses numerous techniques, but when applied to the face, gentleness is paramount. The skin and muscles of the face are delicate structures with rich blood supply — excessive pressure can damage the skin and capillaries. I have developed a set of massage techniques suitable for home self-care based on clinical experience.
Basic Massage Techniques

Pushing (Tui Fa): Using the pads of the index and middle fingers, push upward and outward along the meridian direction with gentle pressure that does not pull the skin. Rubbing (Rou Fa): Make gentle, slow circular motions over acupoints with the fingertip pads — the speed should not be too fast. Pressing (An Fa): Press perpendicularly into acupoints using fingertip pads, increasing pressure gradually until a sensation of soreness and distension is felt, hold for 5 to 10 seconds, then release slowly. Wiping (Mo Fa): Using the pads of the index and middle fingers, wipe along facial contours in straight or curved lines — commonly used for lifting facial contours. Tapping (Pai Fa): Alternately tap the face with both palms or fingertips at a brisk but gentle pace for 30 to 60 seconds — this effectively promotes facial blood circulation.
Facial Massage Steps

I recommend a seven-step facial massage routine. Step one: thoroughly cleanse the face and apply sufficient massage oil or cream to reduce friction. Step two: using the index and middle fingers together, push from the center of the chin along the jawline up to the front of the ear, repeating 10 times — this lifts the jawline contour. Step three: push from both sides of the nose across the cheekbones toward the temples, repeating 10 times. Step four: massage Sibai and Yingxiang points with the index fingertip, 18 rotations each. Step five: massage Taiyang and Cuanzhu points, 18 rotations each. Step six: gently tap the entire face from forehead to jaw for 30 seconds. Step seven: apply a warm towel compress to the face for 1 to 2 minutes to promote blood circulation and enhance skincare product absorption. The complete routine takes approximately 10 to 15 minutes and should be performed once daily.
Massage for Different Problems
The beauty of facial massage lies in its adaptability — different problems require different massage strategies, following the principle of "tailoring treatment to the individual and the condition."
Wrinkle-Fading Massage

From a TCM perspective, wrinkles signal qi and blood depletion leading to undernourished skin. For periorbital wrinkles, focus on massaging Cuanzhu and Sizhukong, combined with gentle pushing from the inner to outer canthus with the index finger. For forehead wrinkles, push alternately upward from Yintang to the hairline using fingertip pads. For drooping mouth corners and perioral lines, focus on Dicang point combined with pushing from the nasolabial groove outward toward both mouth corners. For nasolabial folds — a common concern among middle-aged individuals — push from the base of the nose wing downward along the nasolabial groove toward the mouth corner, repeated multiple times. When these techniques are practiced five or more times weekly, improvements in skin texture are generally observable within about a month.
Whitening & Spot-Fading Massage

Pigmentation spots are often associated with liver stagnation and blood stasis. The goal of massage is to disperse qi and blood stagnation in the face. Sibai is the foremost whitening point — massage until a sensation of soreness and distension is achieved. Quanliao should be massaged with focused attention on pigmented areas. Yingxiang massage improves overall complexion. Additionally, pushing from the center of the face outward along meridian directions helps disperse stagnation and promote metabolism. It should be noted that spot-fading massage requires patience — consistent practice for at least three months is typically needed before results become visible. However, once achieved, the effects are stable and long-lasting, which is difficult to match with topical whitening products.
Puffiness-Eliminating Massage

Morning facial puffiness is most often caused by sluggish fluid metabolism. The key principle for de-puffing massage is "from inside to outside, from bottom to top" — pushing from the facial midline outward and from the jaw upward toward the temples, combined with gentle tapping of the face, effectively promotes lymphatic drainage and fluid metabolism. For puffy under-eye bags, massage periocular acupoints combined with gentle wiping from the inner to outer canthus. After 5 to 10 minutes of consistent massage, puffiness typically subsides noticeably.
Facial Massage Precautions

Though facial massage appears simple, improper technique can be counterproductive. Pressure must be moderate — too heavy may strain the skin or rupture capillaries, while too light fails to stimulate the meridians effectively. Direction must follow the meridian pathways and lymphatic drainage routes, generally adhering to the principle of "upward and outward" — never massage against these directions. Each session should last 10 to 15 minutes; longer sessions may burden the skin. A frequency of once or twice daily is sufficient — excessive frequency offers no additional benefit. Always cleanse the face thoroughly and apply a lubricating medium (massage oil or face cream) before massage to prevent dry friction from damaging the skin.
Best Massage Times

There are two optimal times for facial massage. The first is after waking in the morning — when the body's yang qi is beginning to rise and facial qi and blood are calm after a night's rest, moderate massage awakens facial circulation and refreshes the spirit. The second is one hour before bedtime — evening massage combined with skincare products both relaxes facial nerves (promoting better sleep) and enhances the absorption of active ingredients. Additionally, when experiencing eye strain from prolonged computer use or general fatigue, a brief 5-minute massage of Taiyang and Yintang points can rapidly relieve facial tension. It is worth noting that facial massage should be avoided within 30 minutes after meals and when the skin has acute inflammation or open wounds.

Note: Facial massage requires consistent, long-term practice to achieve visible results — sporadic efforts will not yield satisfactory outcomes. Avoid massage when the skin has severe acne, dermatitis, allergies, or open wounds. For best results, combine facial massage with internal constitutional regulation — true beauty comes from balancing both internal and external approaches.
